_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] The essential air quality apps to help you navigate wildfire season
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

’Tis the season for breathing—and, in many parts of the world, wondering if the air you’re inhaling is going to cause problems.

With my family approaching our one-year anniversary of living in California, wildfires and air quality are all-too-real elements of our day-to-day life. But the reality is that air quality travels—and even if you don’t live somewhere that’s dry and prone to that type of activity, the quality of the air around you can vary wildly based on what’s happening both near and surprisingly far. It also fluctuates based on factors that have nothing to do with fires, like pollen and other common allergen levels.

Living here has been a real wake-up call for me about the realities of air quality—and that’s led me to do a whole bunch o’ searching, testing, and experimenting to find the best tools for tracking air quality and knowing when there’s cause for concern.

The tools I want to share with you today are the result of that experience. And regardless of where you live, they’re well worth your while to keep around and lean on so that you’re aware of the air around you.

This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence. Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of useful tech treasures!

Your air quality eye in the sky

First things first: Most weather apps and services have some manner of air quality indication as a part of their forecasts.

But the apps I’m gonna share with you here are specifically and entirely about air quality, as their primary purpose and measure—and they go above and beyond what most other sources can offer in their detail, their features, and the reliability of the info they provide.

⌚ They’re free, too, and they’ll take you all of 20 seconds to get going.

➜ I rely on a combination of two apps that are perfectly complementary and serve their own specific purposes:

1️⃣ First, for those of us in the States, the official Environmental Protection Agency AirNow app is a solid starting point for official government-measured air quality data.

You can install it on ​Android​ or iOS​ and also access the same info ​on the web​ on any device.

AirNow is where I look to see broad quality reports for our area as well as historical and future forecasting info. It’s great for that big picture kind of info about anywhere you live and how much you need to adjust your outdoor exposure based on conditions.

🌏 For folks outside of the U.S., many other countries offer similar equivalents: 

  • The European Air Quality Index is the same basic idea as the EPA app, only for cities in that part of the world. It’s available on the web​ as well as in app form for both Android​ and ​iOS​.
  • Canada has its WeatherCAN app—for ​Android​ and ​iOS​—that offers general forecast info along with air quality alerts.
  • And Australia has AirRater—also for ​Android​ and ​iOS​—that’s filled with all sorts of useful tools for tracking air quality.

2️⃣ The second app and the one I’ve really come to appreciate and rely on is AirVisual by IQAir.

You can access all of its info on the web​, but its mobile apps (for both ​Android​ and iOS​) are where it shines the brightest.

AirVisual combines official government measurements with hyperlocal sensors set up by regular ol’ folks all around the world to create its own superspecific air quality score for your exact area—often zeroing right down into your neighborhood for a much more meaningful assessment than what the broad view alone can tell you.

It leans on a sprawling global network of simple outdoor sensors​ that people purchase and set up to monitor the air quality and report back constant readings—which AirVisual uses as a part of its formula for calculating your air quality. (You can even opt to purchase your own sensor if you want to go all out and have a reading right outside your home, but there are enough other sensors out and about in the world that it’s not typically necessary to get a meaningful measure.)

The AirVisual app has a nice widget that makes it extra easy to check in on current quality near you, and it can be set up to show you both once-daily alerts and customizable alerts when quality levels drop below a certain concerning level.

Along with AirNow or your regional equivalent, it makes for a powerful one-two punch of air quality awareness—one that can keep you informed at whatever level you like and let you breathe easy knowing you’ll always be aware of the air around you.

  • AirNow is available and in native app form for both ​Android​ and ​iOS​. AirVisual also exists ​on the web​ and as an app for both Android​ and ​iOS​.
  • They’re completely free to use. AirVisual offers the option to purchase your own personal sensor if (and only if!) you want.
  • AirNow doesn’t require any unusual permissions or any accounts, and the app says it doesn’t collect or share any sort of personal data. AirVisual requires an account only if you want to add in your own sensor or use customized alerts, and it also says it doesn’t collect or share any sort of user info.

Treat yourself to all sorts of practical treasures like this with the free Cool Tools newsletter—starting with an instant introduction to an incredible audio app that’ll tune up your days in truly delightful ways.

items.title: [Macworld] Apple lays off 200 employees to focus on ‘new devices’ and AI
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

According to a report by Bloomberg, Apple is laying off and “realigning” several employees in multiple departments in order to “focus on new devices and artificial intelligence.” About 200 employees are affected.

The Vision Pro team has eliminated 100 jobs, with most of the cuts happening in teams focused on gaming and immersive video, according to the report. Bloomberg says employees were told that the changes are being made to better address how the Vision Pro is being used by its customers. Immersive video, in particular, is an expensive endeavor that has “strained the business given the limited number of active Vision Pro users.”

The other 100 eliminated jobs were from the Siri and software teams. With the shift from Siri as a voice-activated interface to the new Siri AI, Apple needs to redefine the Siri team with “a change in the necessary expertise.” Apple is also reorganizing its Intelligent Systems Experience team to focus its efforts on AI.

In response to the report, Apple released the following statement to Bloomberg:

While we will create new roles as part of this change, it will also impact a limited number of existing roles. We are grateful to these team members for their contributions, and we are committed to supporting them throughout their transition, including opportunities to apply for other roles at Apple.

Apple statement released to Bloomberg

While job cuts are never a good sign, no one would be surprised by Apple’s reasoning behind them. The Vision Pro was released over two years ago (with an M5 update in October 2025), and if it has made an impact, it’s in specific niche markets–it has not made an impression with the general public. Reports have said that Apple shifted its focus from developing a low-cost Vision Pro headset to smart glasses that would compete with the likes of Meta.

The only thing surprising about the layoffs with the Siri team is that they didn’t happen sooner. Siri AI has been in development for quite some time now, so a reorganization seems to be part of the process.

items.title: [Fast Company] Apple and Amazon users: Beware this new ‘unauthorized charge’ scam
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

It seems like hardly a month goes by without some new or increasingly frequent online scam trying to separate us from our money or data. In June, it was the so-called Apple High Alert scam. Now it’s a swindle using both Apple and Amazon as its facade. Here’s what you need to know about the Apple and Amazon “unauthorized charge” scam—and how to protect yourself.

What is the Apple and Amazon “unauthorized charge” scam?

The scam is a phishing scheme designed to get unsuspecting targets to hand over their personal details and/or money. Phishing is the practice scammers use to impersonate legitimate organizations in hopes of extracting sensitive information or payment details from you.

The scam involves displaying a malicious pop-up in your browser that purports to be a notification from Apple or Amazon. The scam was recently highlighted by the cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes, which says the scam is delivered by compromised websites, browser redirects, or malicious ads that take a user to a website that looks like Apple’s or Amazon’s in the background. In the foreground, a pop-up will appear that matches the design language of Apple or Amazon.

The pop-up warns that a suspicious pre-authorized payment of $149.99 has been detected on your Apple or Amazon account. It then directs you to call the phone number shown in the pop-up if you did not authorize the charge, to speak with an Apple or Amazon representative, ostensibly to protect your account.

How does the scam work?

The scam works by following certain design and psychological principles.

On the design side, the pop-ups are meant to look like legitimate ones you would see from Apple or Amazon (with rounded corners and blue buttons on the Apple decoys, for example). These pop-ups also have a transparent background that shows what is apparently Apple’s or Amazon’s real website behind them, though this is usually just a screenshot or a cloned site. The point is, the pop-ups are designed to make things look as genuine as possible.

Then come the psychological tricks. The scammers know that most people have an Apple or Amazon account, which means if you see a notification from either company, you are likely to pay it at least some attention. Once the fake notification has your attention, it uses the usual phishing tricks: creating a sense of urgency by claiming that your account or payment method may be compromised and that you need to act immediately, often by calling a phone number, to protect it.

Of course, if you call the phone number, you’ll actually be talking to a scammer who will try to extract personal details from you, like your login, password, payment details, name, address, or more. Alternatively, the scammer may try to get you to make a payment with a credit card or gift card to “protect your account.”

As Malwarebytes notes, the suspicious $149.99 charge that the notification warns about also holds psychological sway. It’s a realistic amount for a product sold on Amazon or a yearly subscription sold on Apple’s App Store. The plausible amount gets you to lower your defenses, making you think, What if this is legit?

How do I know if I am the target of the “unauthorized charge” scam?

The best way to know if you are being targeted by the scam is to pay attention to where the supposed notification appears. 

You should be suspicious of any notification that suddenly appears in your web browser, regardless of whether it’s on mobile or desktop. As noted by Malwarebytes, Apple and Amazon don’t alert you about account or payment issues via browser pop-ups. They’ll send you emails, in-app notifications, or activity log alerts in your account instead.

Another big tell is that the pop-up notifications often direct you to call a phone number, which Amazon and Apple won’t do. You should also be on the lookout for any doom-mongering messaging in the alert, such as threats that failure to act can leave you financially or legally liable. These are frequent tells that the notification isn’t genuine, no matter how authentic it looks.

How can I protect myself against the scam?

Never click on a web-browser pop-up that alleges to be an urgent notification telling you that your account or payment details were compromised. 

If there is actually an unauthorized pending charge on your Amazon or Apple account, those companies likely won’t be the only ones who know about it—your bank or credit card company will, too. So if you see a notification that says someone is trying to make, or has made, a payment you didn’t authorize, you can simply check with your bank or credit card company to see if any charges are pending. You can also close your browser, navigate to Apple or Amazon’s real website, log in to your account, and see any pending charges there.

Finally, often you can easily identify that a notification is a scam by noting the phone number it tells you to call, then simply Googling that number or entering it into one of the many online tools that track scam numbers, like Scamwise or Malwarebytes’s Scam Number Check website.
